notes: Fiscal year 2026 runs Oct 1, 2025 to Sept 30, 2026 (school district: July 1, 2025 to June 30, 2026).

property_tax_dollars = gross taxes levied at the adopted millage, from the Florida Department of Revenue 2025 'Comparison of Levies' Table 1 for Bay County. Budgeted ad valorem revenue (usually about 95% of the levy) appears separately in gf_revenues where available.

Unless a 'status' field says otherwise, figures are from adopted/final documents. All dollar figures are nominal. Group totals marked 'grouped' were summed by the researcher from line items in the cited source; nothing was estimated.

governments.name: Bay County Board of County Commissioners

fy2026.status: adopted at final hearing Sept 16, 2025 (budget book still labels columns 'Tentative/Recommended'; final hearing presentation confirms these totals were adopted)
fy2026.gf_expenditures_note: Grouped by researcher from department totals in the FY2026 Final Budget Commissioners' Book General Fund proforma; groups sum to $281,737,981.
fy2026.source_title: Bay County FY 2026 Final Budget Commissioners' Book (Sept 16, 2025); FY 2026 Final Budget Revenue Detail Report; FY 2026 Final Budget Hearing Presentation

context.text: The countywide general millage stayed at 5.4362 mills for FY2026, the same rate since FY2024. FY2021 through FY2023 used 4.4362 mills; the FY2024 budget raised it by 1.0 mill.

Commissioners turned down a staff proposal to raise the fire MSTU rate slightly and kept it at 1.38 mills. Part of the cost of new fire apparatus will come from reserves instead, and a Tourist Development Council partnership helps pay for lifeguards.

The aggregate adopted rate (6.1067 mills) was 1.81% above the aggregate rolled-back rate (5.9982), so under Florida's TRIM rules it counts as a tax increase even though the millage rates did not change.

The county says roughly $27 million (about 16.5%) of the countywide property taxes it collects goes to Community Redevelopment Agencies run by the cities. That includes an annual payment of about $22.2 million to Panama City Beach's Front Beach Road CRA. The county also says that about 44.7% of its roughly $164 million in General Fund property tax supports the Sheriff, the jail and EMS.

On a county information page that takes no position, Bay County estimates that statewide Amendment 3 (November 2026 ballot: a larger non-school homestead exemption and a lower assessment cap on non-homestead property) would reduce its recurring revenue by about $22M in FY2027-28 and about $36M in FY2028-29.
The FY2026 budget adds 25 net new authorized positions: 835 total, up from 810 in FY2025.

context.text: The total millage rose slightly, from 5.311 to 5.337. Coverage at the tentative stage described it as the first increase in six years and 0.99% above the rolled-back rate. The state sets the Required Local Effort portion (3.089 mills), which the district reported would yield about $104.5M toward FEFP funding.

Amendment 3 on the November 2026 ballot would not change the exemption that applies to school property taxes.

context.text: The commission kept the 4.7999 mill rate (also used in FY2023). News coverage said the city cut about $8 million in spending and gave the budget as about $136 million, which is the total excluding interfund transfers.
The adopted rate is 3.2% above the rolled-back rate (4.6529).
The General Fund pays a $1.84M grant to the city's Community Redevelopment Agency. The St. Andrews CRA fund ($1.68M) and Downtown CRA fund ($0.58M) are budgeted separately.

fy2026.millage_note: The city levies no ad valorem property tax. It relies mainly on Business Tax Receipts.

context.text: Panama City Beach levies no city property tax. Its Front Beach Road CRA receives tax-increment payments, mainly from Bay County (about $22.2M a year, according to the county). The FY2026 budget lists a $22.2M reimbursement from the CRA trust fund.
The council approved the budget unanimously. News coverage cited a general budget of about $72 million, with law enforcement as the largest item at nearly $23 million.
